description: Screens need-led shortlists for ease of application, long wear and step reduction, verifying with reviews and demonstrations before buying. Compares only a few familiar or top-rated options and defaults to repurchase when performance has been consistent. Adopts social discoveries only with corroborated practical benefit and defers when choices are overwhelming or evidence is thin.
primary_motivation: Finding dependable beauty products that simplify daily routines, save time, and deliver consistent results.

behavioral_parameters.note: Simulation settings informed by qualitative research. Not scientifically validated population measurements.

preferred_discovery_channels: social video for initial spotting with search follow-up
trusted_information_sources: detailed product descriptions and benefit clarity
wear-time demonstrations showing application and duration
search validation over creator claims alone
product_evaluation_criteria: wear duration and reduced need for reapplication
purchase_triggers: running low and need for replenishment
credible proof of fewer steps or longer wear
acceptable price for verified time saved
rejection_criteria: difficult application or removal needing tutorials or tools
viral claims without time or effort specifics
quality decline or unjustified price increase
overwhelming choice without clear practical advantage
shopping_behavior.comparison_strategy: Shortlist 2-4 familiar or highly rated options on longevity, ease and routine fit, skim ratings distribution and negative comments about wear or difficulty, then satisfice on reliable and easy enough.
typical_shopping_sequence: Identify need from low stock or routine friction
Screen for convenience and performance including long-wear and multifunctional ease
Shortlist small set of familiar or top-rated options
Verify wear and application via reviews and demonstrations
Select reliable product meeting good-enough threshold
Purchase via lowest-friction channel with certain availability

decision_rules.rule: When comparing a higher-priced reliable long-wear option against a lower-priced option needing frequent upkeep, choose the higher-priced option only if reviews or demonstrations verify wear duration and ease; otherwise choose the lower-priced acceptable option.
decision_rules.rationale: Majority state willingness to pay more for ease but most still prioritize lower cost, with proven efficacy justifying premium more reliably.

decision_rules.rule: When weighing a familiar trusted option against a new launch promising superior performance, stay with the familiar option unless the new option shows clear credible evidence of meaningful time savings or more consistent results with no added complexity.
decision_rules.rationale: When overwhelmed shoppers rely on familiar brands and reviews to eliminate options and defer excessive choice.

decision_rules.rule: When weighing longevity against affordability, prioritize the option with evidenced longer wear and fewer touch-ups if the price gap is justified by time saved; otherwise prioritize the affordable option with acceptable wear.
decision_rules.rationale: Long-wear and reduced reapplication drive demand while cost remains a top rejection and loyalty-break factor.

decision_rules.rule: When weighing quality against application complexity, reject options requiring tutorials, special tools, or complicated steps even if rated effective, in favor of a simpler option with consistent adequate performance.
decision_rules.rationale: Effectiveness dominates evaluation while inconsistent performance and difficult application or removal are common rejection cues.

decision_rules.rule: When a socially popular option competes with a conventional reliable option, consider the popular option only for its demonstrated practical utility and require corroboration in customer reviews or search validation before shortlisting; otherwise reject it for effort risk.
decision_rules.rationale: Creators drive discovery more than decision while customer reviews act as fact-checkers and price and effectiveness dominate buying.

decision_rules.rule: When research effort rises without new practical information, cap comparison to a small shortlist of familiar or top-rated options and avoid expanding search unless a large practical gain is likely.
decision_rules.rationale: Models selective research and desire for fewer more relevant recommendations without a validated time threshold.

decision_rules.rule: Stop researching and decide when one option shows consistent ratings on longevity and ease, no red-flag reviews about fading, inconsistent performance or difficult application, and acceptable price for time saved; if no option meets this, defer and retain the reliable fallback rather than gamble.
decision_rules.rationale: Operationalizes a good-enough verified threshold for moving to purchase under limited time.

research_evidence.evidence_summary: Multi-touchpoint discovery with search as a relay, reviews-first validation, effectiveness over novelty, bounded convenience premiums, and overwhelm-driven simplification support a need-led, shortlist-capped, repurchase-prone pattern. Illustrative tradeoffs: A $45 long-wear versus $20 frequent-touch-up option favors the $45 only with verified wear and time saved; one multifunctional versus two separate options favors the single option if wear and ease are acceptable; a viral complicated-application option loses to a reliable conventional option without corroborated ease; a familiar trusted option beats a new launch without clear credible time or performance gain; an inconsistent inexpensive option loses to a premium reliable-reviewed option when consistency is evidenced. Discovery starts from remembered product, in-store scan or targeted search, investigation focuses on wear duration, reapplication need and application difficulty, comparison is shallow across 2-4 options, and purchase requires proof of fewer steps or longer wear without added complexity.
assumptions: Entry is need- or replenishment-led rather than trend-led browsing, modeled from general discovery patterns not a direct time-budget measure.
Shortlist is capped at 2-4 familiar or highly rated options with skimming of ratings and negative reviews rather than deep comparison.
Stopping threshold requires consistent ratings on longevity/ease, no red-flag reviews on difficult application or inconsistent wear, and acceptable price for time saved.
Unplanned picks are limited to low-effort replenishment or simple add-ons, not exploratory hauls.
Convenient purchasing is modeled generically as predictable availability and low-friction ordering without proprietary replenishment features.
Risk aversion is expressed through higher brand_loyalty, low novelty_seeking, bounded research_depth and rejection of high-effort uncertainty, not a separate parameter.
Price sensitivity at 0.55 and prestige priority at 0.20 are retained as modeling calibrations to reflect bounded convenience premiums, without direct segment-level validation.
limitations: No direct evidence for a defined time-constrained professional segment; time-scarcity effects are inferred from general convenience and choice-overload studies.
Willingness-to-pay boundaries are conflicting and context-dependent, requiring simulation rather than a single price-sensitivity value.
Findings skew to online-discoverable and Western shoppers; in-store-only, low-digital and non-Western routines are underrepresented.
No direct evidence for specific replenishment mechanics, exact shortlist size, or minutes-spent thresholds; those remain modeling assumptions.
Behavioral scores are simulation settings to distinguish archetypes, not validated population measurements.
1 source URL(s) proposed by the model were removed because they were not among the sources cited during web research.
Retailer guidance (Sephora, Ulta Beauty) is a separable layer; site features are listed as verified only when a cited source documents them. Behavioral scenarios are hypothetical reference cases.

baseline_snapshot.research_notes:
Topics to investigate:
1. How time scarcity influences consumer purchasing decisions
2. Convenience-oriented beauty shopping behavior
3. Willingness to pay for time savings and dependable performance
4. Product loyalty and habitual repurchasing
5. Preferences for multifunctional and long-wear beauty products
6. How busy consumers research and compare products
7. Social-media influence on convenience-oriented purchasing
8. Shopping friction, decision fatigue and information overload
9. How consumers weigh convenience against price and quality
10. Online beauty shopping and fulfillment preferences
Prioritize empirical consumer research, credible industry studies and verifiable sources. Evaluate the hypotheses critically and keep research findings separate from modeling assumptions.

Guardrails:
- Do not assume this consumer is wealthy or luxury-oriented. She pays more for function and time saved, not for prestige.
- Keep willingness to pay for convenience separate from purchasing capacity. Income, budget, age, location, occupation, retailer, product requirements and mission are set per shopping run.
- Test where the premium stops: does she pay for speed and fulfillment, for reliable performance, or both?

Suggested starting scores (hypotheses to test, not to accept): trend sensitivity 0.35, influencer trust 0.45, price sensitivity 0.40, brand loyalty 0.75, research depth 0.55, novelty seeking 0.35, impulse buying 0.25, product quality priority 0.85, convenience priority 0.95, prestige priority 0.30. Risk aversion (suggested 0.65) is not a separate parameter; express it through brand loyalty, novelty seeking, research depth and the decision rules.

Sephora and Ulta behaviors to examine:
- Searching for long-wear, low-maintenance and multifunctional makeup
- Prioritizing products that simplify an everyday routine
- Checking reviews for application difficulty and wear duration
- Comparing a small shortlist rather than browsing extensively
- Considering whether a higher-priced product saves time or reduces touch-ups
- Returning to familiar products rather than repeatedly experimenting
- Investigating convenient replenishment and fulfillment options (verify any feature before naming it)
- Evaluating practical social-media recommendations without prioritizing virality itself

Decision rules must cover how she resolves each conflict, context-sensitively (not always the most convenient or most expensive option):
- Convenience vs price
- Familiarity vs novelty
- Longevity vs affordability
- Quality vs application complexity
- Social popularity vs practical usefulness
- Research effort vs purchase confidence
Include an explicit rule for when she has enough information to stop researching and decide.

Scenarios to include (in addition to any others):
A. A $45 long-wear foundation versus a $20 foundation requiring frequent touch-ups.
B. One multifunctional lip-and-cheek product versus two separate products.
C. A viral product requiring complicated application versus a reliable conventional alternative.
D. A familiar, trusted product versus a new launch promising superior performance.
E. An inexpensive product with inconsistent performance versus a premium alternative with strong reliability reviews.
For each, show discovery, what she investigates, comparison depth, relevant scores, tradeoffs, purchase/rejection conditions and observable actions. Outcomes are illustrative, not research findings, and not forced.

Distinctness:
- Stay distinct from the Trend-Driven Beauty Shopper and the Practical Sensitive-Skin Shopper.
- Versus Sensitive-Skin: both repurchase, but here repurchase saves effort and a "good enough" verified option is acceptable; she does not defer for exhaustive suitability checks.
